title: Can there be objective morality without God?
realQuestion:
Torturing a child for entertainment is wrong. Not disapproved of, not counter-productive — wrong, and it would still have been wrong if everyone alive had approved.

The question is what makes that true, and the reason this argument goes badly so often is that neither side has one answer. Christians disagree with each other about whether morality is grounded in God's commands, in the natures he made, or in neither; atheists disagree with each other about whether there are moral facts at all. So an objection aimed at one version routinely sails past the person it is aimed at, who holds another.

Both sides are set out here with their internal divisions visible, because those divisions are what decides whether any given objection has hit anything.

distinctions.label: Can someone be good without believing in God?
distinctions.gloss: Yes, and no serious participant denies it. A question about psychology, not about grounding, and confusing the two is the most common failure in this argument. Set aside.

distinctions.label: Does objective morality require God?
distinctions.gloss: This is the argument on this page: whether theism is needed to account for moral facts, and what happens to the argument if there turn out not to be any.

distinctions.label: Which metaethical theory is actually true?
distinctions.gloss: A much larger question, and not this one. Several of the positions below could be right without settling whether God is required — the page asks only about that dependence, and takes each position at its own word about the rest. Set aside.

glossary.definition: The view that some moral claims are true independently of what anyone thinks or feels. Held by most, but not all, of the positions on this page.
The account on which moral obligations are constituted by God's commands. The modern version adds that God's own nature constrains what he can command.
The older Christian alternative, from Aquinas: what is good for a creature follows from the kind of creature it is, so morality is grounded in natures and knowable by reason.
Mackie's view that ordinary moral claims assert objective values, that there are none, and that our moral talk is therefore systematically false rather than merely subjective.
The argument that if our evaluative attitudes were shaped by selection for fitness rather than for truth, we have no account of why they would track moral facts, whatever those facts are.

sides.label: Obligation is owed to someone, and particles are owed nothing

arguments.claim: A duty is something you owe, and owing is a relation between persons
arguments.explanation:
The best-known Christian account distinguishes two things usually run together. Values are about what is good; duties are about what you must do. Robert Adams' version, which is the serious form, grounds the first in God's nature — God is the standard that finite goods resemble — and the second in his commands.

The force is in the second half. You can be told that cruelty is bad and reasonably ask why that binds you. A moral requirement has the structure of a demand, and a demand is made by someone. That is the version of the argument almost everyone meets, and it is not the only one Christians hold: two alternatives are set out below, and they ground obligation in something other than a command.

quote.text: If God does not exist, objective moral values do not exist.
quote.author: William Lane Craig
quote.work: the first premise of the moral argument, as Craig states it
quote.locator: Craig defines 'objective' as 'valid and binding independently of whether anybody believes in it or not'

variants.label: Divine command
variants.heldBy: Robert Adams, Philip Quinn, C. Stephen Evans, William Lane Craig
variants.oneLine: Obligations are constituted by God's commands; his nature constrains what he can command, so they are not arbitrary.
variants.summary: The main argument above in its developed modern form. Ockham's version — right is right because commanded, and God could have commanded cruelty — has few modern defenders. Adams' modified theory splits the work: the good is grounded in God's nature, which he does not choose, and obligation is grounded in the commands of a God who is by nature loving. That is what is supposed to answer the Euthyphro dilemma without conceding a standard above God.

quote.text: since our moral duties are constituted by God's commands, what He commands is just and right
quote.author: William Lane Craig
quote.work: Slaughter of the Canaanites (Question of the Week)

variants.changesTheObjection: It does not. This is the version the objection above is built against, and the one it reaches: if obligation is constituted by a command, the question of why you are obliged to obey has to be answered without appealing to another command. Everything below is a way of not being in that position.

variants.label: Natural law
variants.heldBy: Thomas Aquinas; John Finnis, Edward Feser; Catholic moral teaching
variants.oneLine: The good for a creature follows from what kind of creature it is, so morality is grounded in natures and reachable by reason without revelation.
variants.summary:
The older and, across Christian history, the more widely held account. Obligation is not imposed by a decree but follows from what a thing is for: reason apprehends that certain ends are good for a being of this kind, and the first precept of practical reason follows from that apprehension rather than from an instruction.

One consequence matters for this page. On natural law, an atheist can know the content of morality perfectly well, because it is read off natures rather than off revelation — which is why the tradition has never had trouble saying that unbelievers know right from wrong.

quote.text: good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. All other precepts of the natural law are based upon this
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.locator: the first precept of the natural law

variants.changesTheObjection: The regress cannot start. There is no command whose authority needs a prior obligation to obey, because obligation follows from what a creature is rather than from what it has been told. The Euthyphro dilemma also loses its grip here: God is not consulting an external standard and not choosing one either, since he is the author of the natures the standard is read off.

variants.label: Moral concurrentism
variants.oneLine: Neither commands nor natures alone: facts about God and facts about creatures cooperate, and moral necessity is the pull of divine goodness as specified by what you are.
variants.summary:
The most recent of the three, and it exists because its author thinks the other two both fail as explanations. Murphy argues that divine command theory cannot account for why God's commands bind, and that natural law does not keep God in the explanation at all — a theory on which the moral law would be exactly the same whether or not God existed is not a theistic explanation of morality, whatever its proponents intend.

His alternative has the two doing different jobs at once: God's goodness supplies the pull, and the nature of the creature determines what that pull requires of it.

quote.text: all moral necessity is the pull of divine goodness specified by the nature of the creatures involved
quote.author: Mark C. Murphy
quote.work: God and Moral Law: On the Theistic Explanation of Morality
quote.locator: the thesis of moral concurrentism, quoted in the Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews notice

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection has to find a command to regress on, and there is none: what necessitates is a pull, not an instruction, so asking why you must obey it is like asking why you must find the good good. What the objection can do instead is press the other way — whether a 'pull' that requires no acknowledgement is doing any work that the natures were not already doing.

counter.objection: If an obligation is constituted by a command, then being commanded to do something makes it obligatory only if you are already obliged to do what you are commanded. That prior obligation cannot itself be constituted by a command without starting the regress again, so it must come from somewhere else — and once something else can generate an obligation, the account has conceded the point it was making. This is not the atheist's objection; it is the standing objection made inside theism by those who ground morality elsewhere.
counter.sharedPremise: it accepts that God exists, that he is good, and that moral facts are real, and argues from those premises alone that obligations cannot be constituted by commands, since obeying a command is obligatory only given a prior obligation to obey — a premise the divine command theorist grants.
counter.response: The prior obligation is not a further command but a feature of the relationship: a creature stands to its creator as a child to a parent, and the obligation to heed is part of what that relation is rather than a rule inside it.

arguments.claim: On naturalism our moral sense was built for survival, which gives no reason to think it tracks moral truth
arguments.explanation:
This is the epistemological half, and it targets the other side's strongest position rather than a weak one. Grant that there are objective moral facts standing on their own. Now ask how creatures like us came to know any of them.

Our moral responses were shaped by selection, and selection rewards what works, not what is true. A tendency to protect your children is favoured whether or not there is a mind-independent fact that you ought to. This is the [[evolutionary debunking]] argument turned to theist use: the naturalist realist has beliefs whose reliability they cannot account for, while a theist can, since faculties made by a moral being might be expected to track moral reality.

quote.text: The naturalist must hold that human moral faculties were shaped by selection for reproductive fitness rather than for tracking mind-independent moral truth, and so has no account of their reliability; the theist, taking those faculties to be created by a good God, does.
quote.author: Mark D. Linville
quote.work: The Moral Argument, in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology
quote.locator: our summary of the evolutionary argument against naturalistic moral realism, pp. 391-448; not Linville's wording. At the top of VERIFICATION.md for a primary check

counter.objection: The argument cuts against its user. If selection shaped our moral faculties, it shaped them whether or not God exists — God would have had to work through the same process, so the theist inherits the identical story about how the beliefs arrived and has only added a hope about where it was heading. And the reliability challenge has an answer available: if some moral truths are necessary, then any process producing beliefs about cooperation, harm and fairness will produce beliefs that are true, not by luck but because those truths could not have been otherwise.
counter.response: That reply needs the necessary truths to line up with what was adaptive, which is the coincidence the argument was pointing at rather than an explanation of it.

sides.label: Nothing is added by putting a person underneath

arguments.claim: Moral truths, if there are any, need no more of a maker than mathematical ones do
arguments.explanation:
The best-known atheist answer is not that morality is invented or a matter of feeling. It is that there are objective normative truths, that they are not reducible to natural facts, and that they stand without anything having made them so — the same status the theist has always been willing to grant to God.

The argument is one of parity. The theist stops at a being whose goodness is not explained by anything further; the realist stops one step earlier, at the truths themselves. Neither can say why their stopping point is there, and only one of them is accused of leaving something out. Derek Parfit's version adds a twist that makes the parity sharper: the truths are real and objective while carrying no ontological weight at all, so there is nothing extra in the universe for the theist to demand an account of.

Atheists divide here, and the divisions matter more than the agreement — one of the versions below is an [[error theory]] that denies there are any moral facts, and agrees with the theist's first premise.

quote.text: there are some claims that are irreducibly normative in the reason-involving sense, and are in a strong sense true. These truths have no ontological implications.
quote.author: Derek Parfit
quote.locator: the position Parfit calls Non-Metaphysical Non-Naturalist Normative Cognitivism

variants.label: Robust non-natural realism
variants.heldBy: David Enoch, Erik Wielenberg, Russ Shafer-Landau
variants.oneLine: There are irreducibly normative facts, independent of anyone's will, and they are as real as the theist's God is.
variants.summary:
The full-strength version of the main argument, and the one that takes on the most metaphysical commitment rather than the least. Where Parfit tries to keep objectivity without ontology, Enoch and Wielenberg accept the ontology and defend it: there really are non-natural moral properties out there, and the awkwardness of that is the price of taking morality seriously.

Wielenberg presses the parity point hardest, arguing that a theist who accepts brute necessary facts about God's nature has no standing to object to brute necessary facts about goodness.

quote.text: there are irreducibly normative truths and facts … [they] are independent of us, our desires and our (or anyone else's) will
quote.author: David Enoch
quote.work: Taking Morality Seriously: A Defense of Robust Realism

variants.changesTheObjection: It does not. This is the version the debunking objection is built against and reaches most directly: facts that are causally inert and independent of us are exactly the facts it is hardest to explain our tracking. The two positions below are ways of not owning facts of that kind.

variants.label: Naturalist realism
variants.heldBy: Sam Harris; the Cornell realists — Richard Boyd, Peter Railton, Nicholas Sturgeon
variants.oneLine: Moral facts are natural facts — about wellbeing, flourishing, what conscious creatures suffer — so they are objective and discoverable in the ordinary way.
variants.summary:
This version refuses the non-natural ontology and the mystery that comes with it. If moral claims are ultimately claims about the wellbeing of conscious creatures, then they are true or false the way claims about health are, and no special faculty of moral perception is needed to reach them.

It is the most popular position outside philosophy and among the more contested inside it: the standard objection, from Moore onwards, is that any identification of goodness with a natural property leaves it open to ask whether that property is good — which is not a question you can ask about a genuine identity.

quote.text: Questions about values … are really questions about the well-being of conscious creatures.
quote.author: Sam Harris
quote.work: The Moral Landscape: How Science Can Determine Human Values

variants.changesTheObjection: The debunking argument has to be restated and loses much of its force. If moral facts are natural facts about what harms and helps creatures like us, then a faculty selected for detecting harm and help to creatures like us is tracking them by construction, and no coincidence needs explaining. What the objection can still press is whether the identification is right — but that is Moore's open question, not a debunking argument.

variants.label: Error theory
variants.oneLine: Ordinary moral claims do assert objective values, there are none, and so moral talk is systematically false — not subjective, false.
variants.summary:
The position most often left out of this argument, and the one that changes it most. Mackie agrees with the theist about what moral language means and about what it would take to make it true: there really would have to be objective values, and they would be very strange entities, unlike anything else we know of. He then denies that there are any.

What that does to the moral argument is worth stating plainly. The usual form runs: if God does not exist, objective moral values do not exist; objective moral values do exist; therefore God exists. Mackie accepts the first premise and denies the second. He is the atheist who agrees with the theist's conditional, which is why an objection built to defend the second premise passes him by entirely.

quote.author: J.L. Mackie
quote.locator: the opening sentence of chapter 1, 'The Subjectivity of Values'

variants.changesTheObjection: There is nothing left for it to do. A debunking argument shows that our moral beliefs are not explained by moral facts; the error theorist agrees, and has been saying so since 1977. Aimed here, the objection is not a refutation but a restatement of the position — and the theist who runs it has to switch to a different argument entirely, one for the existence of the moral facts Mackie denies.

counter.objection: If our evaluative attitudes were shaped by selection, and selection is indifferent to normative truth, then the realist faces a dilemma: either those attitudes are unrelated to the independent truths, in which case we have no reason to think ours are the accurate ones, or the realist owes a tracking account that the independence of the truths makes very hard to give. This is not a theist objection — it is made from naturalism, against other naturalists, and it is the most-cited challenge to atheist realism of the last twenty years.
counter.sharedPremise: it accepts naturalism, and the evolutionary account of where our evaluative attitudes came from, and argues from those premises alone that a realist who takes moral truths to be independent of us still owes an account of why our attitudes would track them.
counter.response: The tracking account is available if some moral truths are necessary: a process that produces beliefs about harm, fairness and cooperation produces true ones because those truths could not have been otherwise, not because it was aiming at them.

arguments.claim: Either God's commands track something already good, or goodness is whatever he happens to command
arguments.explanation:
Socrates asked the question two and a half thousand years ago and it has never been retired. Take anything God commands. Either he commands it because it is good, in which case its goodness is independent of him; or it is good because he commands it, in which case anything at all could have been good.

The usual answer is that God's own nature is the standard, so the choice is a false one. The reply is that this relocates the dilemma: either God's nature is good by a standard, or 'good' just means 'like God', which makes 'God is good' say nothing.

quote.text: Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved by the gods?
quote.author: Plato

counter.objection: The third option is not a dodge and is older than the objection to it. Goodness is identified with God's nature, which is neither an arbitrary choice nor an external standard he consults, because a nature is not something anyone selects. That 'God is good' then becomes something like an identity statement is not a defect: 'water is H₂O' is uninformative in the same way and is not thereby empty. And the dilemma has no purchase at all on the natural law version above, where the question was never about what God commands.
counter.response: The identity works only if we can recognise the goodness independently, which is what lets us say the identity holds rather than being stipulated — and that recognition is the independent standard the theist said there was not.

notes.heading: Hume's gap, which both sides claim
notes.text:
Hume observed that arguments slide without warning from statements about what is to statements about what ought to be, and that the step is never justified. Both sides cite this against the other, and both are entitled to.

Against the naturalist: no set of facts about wellbeing or flourishing adds up to an obligation without a premise that already contains one. Against the theist: no set of facts about what God is or commands adds up to an obligation either, without a premise that you ought to do what God commands — and that premise cannot come from another command without circling, which is the objection printed above. The gap is a problem for anyone deriving morality from anything, which is why almost every position on this page ends by positing something foundational rather than deriving it. The exception is the error theorist, who has nothing to posit.

notes.heading: Three things 'objective' can mean
notes.text:
Most cross-talk in this argument is one word doing three jobs. It can mean *not a matter of opinion* — the Nazis were wrong even though they thought otherwise. It can mean *mind-independent* — true whether or not any minds exist. It can mean *grounded in something outside the natural world*.

The first is agreed by everyone here except the error theorist, who denies it and says so. The second is where most of the disagreement is. The third is a theist thesis, and quietly assuming it is what makes the argument look circular from outside: if 'objective' means 'grounded outside nature', then 'objective morality requires something outside nature' is true by definition and proves nothing. When an exchange goes nowhere, it is usually worth asking which of the three each person is using.

whereItStands:
Both positions are held by serious people and neither is close to collapsing. Among philosophers as a whole, moral realism is the majority view and theism is not, which means most moral realists are atheists — a fact that tells against the claim that the combination is unstable, though it is a headcount rather than an argument.

Where the argument has actually moved is the epistemological half. The metaphysical dispute has been static for a long time, with almost every position positing something foundational and none able to justify stopping where it does. But the question of how evolved creatures came to know moral truths has generated real work in the last twenty years, and the most damaging version of that challenge is made by an atheist against other atheists. Wielenberg's books are substantially a response to it.

What is not in dispute, and gets misreported constantly, is whether atheists can be moral. Nobody in this argument thinks otherwise, including the people making the strongest version of the theist case — and the natural law tradition has a positive account of why they can.
commonMistake:
Christians most often let the argument slide from 'atheism cannot ground morality' to 'atheists have no morals', which is a different claim, is false, and is refuted by every decent unbeliever the listener knows. The second most common is treating divine command theory as the Christian position, when the tradition's older and more widely held answer is natural law, which grounds morality in natures and expects unbelievers to know right from wrong perfectly well.

Atheists most often answer with an account of where our moral feelings came from — evolution, culture, empathy — as though that addressed the question. It does not: an explanation of why we believe cruelty is wrong is compatible with its being wrong and with its not being. And the version of the atheist position most often defended in public is one Mackie spent a book denying, which is worth knowing before defending it.

Both sides also treat their own stopping point as reasonable and the other's as arbitrary. God, uncaused and good by nature, and moral facts, uncaused and true by necessity, are the same move made in two places.
